This post may be a little technical, but for anyone interested in becoming more sophisticated in their thinking, Bayes rule is a handy thing to know. I'll try to make it as simple of an explanation as I can - just basic math. With Pizzagate, we are dealing with probabilities, evidence, and inference, so I believe this is relevant. However, I also think people kind of have an intuitive grasp of this already, even though they don't realize it. Bayes rule is a law of nature, so evolution made sure we have good intuitions here (for the most part).

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayes'_theorem

Basically the rule is this. Let's say "A" is some statement about the world, which could be true or false. Like "the earth revolves around the sun." And say that "e" is the evidence observed, like Tcyho Brahe's observations of the movements of the stars (which formed the basis for Copernicus and Kepler's work). Then

  • Probability(A given e) = [ Probability(e given A) * Probability(A) ] / Probability(e)

What this says basically, is that the probability of A being true, given certain evidence for it, depends on the probability of that evidence being generated if A were true, as well as the prior probability of A (how likely it would be in general, if you didn't have this evidence) and the prior probability of the evidence e. Now when comparing two competing hypotheses, you can drop the latter probability (which can be difficult to calculate, since it involves adding up the probabilities of all the things that could generate e). So if B is the competing hypothesis, "the sun revolves around the earth," you have this comparison:

  • Probability(A given e) = Probability(e given A) * Probability(A) ( > or < ) Probability(e given B) * Probability(B) = Probability(B given e)

So basically, if you want to demonstrate that A is a better hypothesis than B, there are two main strategies:

  • 1) Show that Probability(e given A) is greater than Probability(e given B)
  • (2) Show that Probability(A) > Probability(B)

As this relates to Pizzagate, I would say that the two competing hypothesis are

  • P: there exists a clandestine pedophile ring made up of elites, with activity centered around Comet Ping Pong and Besta Pizza.
  • ~P (not P): there does not exist such a pedophile ring, and all the activity at CPP is just harmless fun

And e is all the evidence we have collected: the instagram photos, the wikileaks emails, etc.

So we just have to show:

  • (1) Probability(e given P) > Probability(e given ~P)
  • (2) Probability(P) > Probability(~P)

With regards to strategy (1), we need to show that a world in which such a pedophile ring exists is more likely to generate this evidence than a world in which this pedophile ring does not exist. The key thing here is that BY DEFINITION you assume that there is a pedophile ring. Your opponent arguing the opposite hypothesis cannot deny you this, at least for this part of the argument. Now, assuming that is true, how likely are we to see this evidence? Assuming that there really is an elite satanic pedophile network, how likely would it be that they would post creepy instagram photos, use code language in their emails, use their influence to have the media cover up for them, have a "kid friendly" venue which also hosts adult entertainment, etc.? Pretty damn likely, don't you think?

Now consider the alternative hypothesis. If there were no such satanic elite pedophile ring, how likely would these people be to post instagram photos of an empty basement with "#murder" as the comment, and a little boy with "#chickenlover"? How likely would they be to host an entertainer who mentions one of the employee's preference for children? How likely would they be to just happen to have logos which are similar to that of known pedophile symbols? How likely would they be to be talking about getting "Pizza for an hour"? The more evidence you list, the lower this probability is.

Now with regards to strategy (2), the key thing here is that we can completely ignore all of the evidence for pizzagate for a second and talk about the broader world we live in. I believe that a major reason why people dismiss Pizzagate is because for them, the prior probability of the existence of an elite pedophile sex ring is very low. Their perspective of reality is skewed by a bought-and-paid-for corporate liberal media, which doesn't report on such things and has no interest in doing so. We have to convince the public that these kinds of things happen, it is not as ridiculous as the MSM is trying to make it out to be.

Another important thing to note, is that if your advantage on one strategy is much greater, you don't necessarily have to "win" on the other strategy. For instance, if Probability(e given P) is much greater than Probability(e given ~P), but Probability(P) is slightly less than Probability(~P), you still have proven your argument, because overall the evidence is in your favor.
